 Enfield fire ant order sets rules for high-risk freight
 Chris Edwards 4 hours ago October 27, 2026 
 A new Biosecurity Control Order around Sydney’s Enfield Intermodal Logistics Centre places conditions on moving specified fire ant carrier materials out of or through a two-kilometre control zone. 
 Image: ANDREY/stock.adobe.com 
 New biosecurity requirements have taken effect around Sydney’s Enfield Intermodal Logistics Centre after a red imported fire ant nest was detected in September.
 The Biosecurity Control Order covers a two-kilometre radius around the logistics precinct and regulates the movement of defined high-risk carrier materials. These include turf, mulch, soil, potted plants and heavy equipment.
 Businesses moving those materials out of or through the control zone must meet treatment and handling requirements before transport. The order does not automatically restrict general freight movements, and it excludes movements that remain entirely within the zone.
 What movements does the order affect?
 The controls apply based on what is being transported, rather than imposing a blanket restriction on vehicles operating around Enfield.
 Businesses carrying defined fire ant carrier materials beyond or through the zone may need to treat or otherwise handle them in accordance with the order before movement.
 The order does not prevent people from travelling through the area or businesses conducting ordinary activities unrelated to controlled materials.
 Why has the control order been introduced?
 The order follows the discovery of a red imported fire ant nest at the Enfield Intermodal Logistics Centre in late September. Biosecurity authorities treated the original nest and began surveillance around the site.
 NSW says it has detected no further fire ants despite almost 400 public reports.
 Nine detection dogs and about 60 personnel have been involved in surveillance, including intensive work within 500 metres of the original detection. The control order establishes a longer-term monitoring and compliance framework following that initial response.
 NSW expects the approach to remain in place for between six and 24 months.
 Why are freight movements part of the response?
 Fire ants can spread when infested material is moved from one location to another. This creates a direct biosecurity issue for transport tasks involving materials that can carry ants or nests.
 The order therefore focuses on moving those materials rather than the logistics precinct itself.
 Operators carrying unaffected freight through Enfield are not subject to a general movement ban under the announcement.
 What must affected businesses do?
 Businesses must first determine whether the material they intend to move falls under the control order.
 If it is, requirements may apply before the load can leave or pass through the control zone.
 NSW biosecurity officers have been visiting businesses within the area to explain the requirements and inspect premises.
 The Government says officers will continue working with affected businesses as the compliance phase proceeds.
 The conditions apply to movements leaving or travelling through the zone, rather than movements entirely within its boundary.
 What happens next at Enfield?
 Surveillance and treatment will continue around the logistics centre and surrounding suburbs as authorities look for evidence of any additional nests.
 The control order provides the regulatory framework for that longer-term response while limiting potential spread through the movement of carrier materials.
 Businesses and drivers who encounter suspected fire ants are being advised not to disturb or treat them.
 Instead, they should photograph the suspected ants or nest, where it is safe to do so, and report the sighting through the NSW Biosecurity Helpline on 1800 680 244 .
